tip: 'Aus' splits off to the end and means off here: 'mache das Licht ... aus' is turn the light off. The base 'machen' alone just means make or do.
'Helfen' acts on a dative object: 'hilft dem Patienten', not 'den Patienten'. A few verbs like 'danken' behave the same way.
'Daumen drücken', literally press thumbs, is German for keeping fingers crossed: 'drücken die Daumen'.
'Innerhalb' takes genitive, but with bare plurals people use 'innerhalb von' plus dative: 'innerhalb von drei Werktagen'.
'In dem' means in which: after a preposition the relative word takes its case, and neuter 'das Hotel' becomes 'dem' in the dative.
'Schwerfallen' takes a dative person: 'anfangs fiel mir die neue Software sehr schwer' means at first I found the new software hard.
'Vertrauen' takes a dative object and no preposition, unlike English trust: 'wir vertrauen unserem Anwalt'.
Feminine nouns mark the genitive with 'seiner' or 'der', not an '-s' ending: 'die Augen seiner Tochter'.
'Zum' is 'zu dem' fused into one word: 'zu' always takes dative, so 'zum Kurs' means to the course, and 'zur Arbeit' does the same for feminine.
'Glauben' uses dative for the person believed: 'er glaubt seinem Sohn nicht'.
'Mir geht es gut' uses dative 'mir' – literally 'to me it goes well'.
'Helfen' takes dative, not accusative: it stays 'dir', not 'dich', in 'ich kann dir leider nicht helfen'.
'Fehlen' flips the English miss: 'sie fehlt ihren Eltern' means she is missing to her parents. The missed person is the subject, the missers go dative.
'Schaden' takes dative where English harm uses a direct object: 'wir schaden der Umwelt'.
Here 'uns' means each other, not us: 'kennen wir uns nicht?' asks don't we know each other.
A few masculine nouns add '-en' outside the nominative: 'der Tourist' becomes 'dem Touristen'.
With two noun objects the dative normally comes before the accusative: 'ich schreibe meiner Oma einen Brief'.
The dative plural normally adds '-n' to the noun itself: 'die Besucher' becomes 'den Besuchern'.
'Antworten' takes a dative person: 'er antwortet dem Lehrer', not 'den Lehrer'.
'Möchte' is a fixed polite I would like: 'ich möchte mich bei Ihnen bedanken' softens the request. Use it when English says I would like.
Verbs of movement or change usually form the perfect with 'sein': 'ist ... geflogen'.
Inseparable 'be-' takes no 'ge-' in the past participle: 'bestehen' becomes 'bestanden'.
'Beim' plus a capitalized verb means while doing it: 'beim Skifahren' is while skiing.
Separable verbs split in a main clause: 'anbieten' becomes 'wir bieten dem Bewerber den Job an'.
The 'der' in 'nach der Reise' is feminine, not masculine: 'die Reise' shifts to 'der' in the dative, which 'nach' always triggers.
The prefix decides the 'ge-': separable 'ein-' keeps it in 'eingesehen', but inseparable 'ent-' drops it in 'entschuldigt', never 'geentschuldigt'.
For your own body part German uses dative 'sich' plus the article: 'sie hat sich ... das Handgelenk verstaucht'.
'Schmecken' takes dative like 'gefallen': 'das Essen schmeckt den Gästen' means it tastes good to the guests.
'Nützen' (to benefit) takes a dative object: 'das Ergebnis nützt dem gesamten Forschungsteam'.
'Eines Geschenks' is genitive because 'anstatt' demands it, not because of possession: 'anstatt', 'wegen' and 'trotz' all normally take the genitive.
